title: Group Anagrams
directAnswer: Group words that are anagrams of each other. The trick is a canonical key shared by all anagrams of a word — either the sorted word or a 26-length character-count signature. Bucket every word into a hash map keyed by that signature, then return the buckets. Sorted key: O(n·k log k); count key: O(n·k), where n = number of words, k = max word length.

rules: All anagrams must collapse to the **same key** — sort the word, or use a tuple of 26 counts.
The count-tuple key is `O(k)` per word vs `O(k log k)` for sorting — faster for long words.
Use the key only to **bucket**; the stored values are the original words, untouched.
Pick a key type your map can hash: a **string** in Java (`new String(count)`), a **tuple** in Python.
Return `map.values()` — order of groups doesn't matter per the problem.
whenToUse: Group / cluster items that share an equivalence (anagram, same digits, same shape)
'Partition this list by some normalized form'
Any time a canonical representative collapses many inputs to one bucket
antiSignals: Just compare two strings → Valid Anagram (no bucketing needed)
Need anagram substrings of a text → sliding-window frequency
Equivalence can't be reduced to a hashable key → may need union-find
remember.takeaway: Bucketing by a canonical key is the go-to for any 'group things that are equivalent' problem. Choosing a cheap, collision-free key (sorted form or count signature) is the whole game.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you invent a canonical key that all anagrams share and use it as a hash-map bucket key — and whether you can improve the key from O(k log k) sorting to O(k) counting.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Comparing every pair of words for anagram-ness (O(n²·k)), or building a key that isn't actually shared by all anagrams.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Offer both keys, explain the count-signature beats sorting for long words, and note the map values are the original words so no information is lost.

problemStatement:
Given an array of strings `strs`, group the anagrams together. You can return the answer in **any order**.

An **anagram** is a word formed by rearranging the letters of another, using all the original letters exactly once.
constraints: strs[i] consists of lowercase English letters
understanding: Cluster the input words so that each cluster contains exactly the words that are rearrangements of one another. We need a way to recognize 'same letters' that's identical for every member of a group.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the order of groups, or words within a group, matter?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — any order is accepted, which is why a hash map (unordered) is fine.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the strings lowercase English only?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes per constraints, so a 26-slot count key is valid. For Unicode you'd key by a map/encoded counts.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can a word be empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — empty strings are anagrams of each other and form their own group under either key.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How long can the words get?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to 100 chars. That makes the O(k) count key meaningfully cheaper than the O(k log k) sort key at scale.

examples.explanation: eat/tea/ate share key 'aet'; tan/nat share 'ant'; bat is alone.
A single empty string forms one group.
A single character is its own group.

approaches.name: Sorted-Word Key
approaches.whenToMention: The cleanest first answer — easy to reason about and to code.
hints: What single value is identical for every anagram of a word, regardless of letter order?
Sorting a word gives a canonical form: 'eat', 'tea', 'ate' all sort to 'aet'.
Use that sorted form as a hash-map key; append each original word to its bucket.
approaches.complexityReasoning: For each of n words we sort k characters (O(k log k)) and do O(1) map work. Total O(n·k log k). We store every word once → O(n·k) space.
approaches.explanation:
For every word, compute its sorted character string and use that as a map key. All anagrams of a word sort to the identical string, so they land in the same bucket. After processing every word, the map's values are exactly the groups.

**Why the sorted form is a valid key.** Sorting is a canonicalization: it maps all permutations of the same multiset of letters to one representative. Two words share a sorted form iff they're anagrams — which is precisely the grouping rule.
approaches.insight: This reuses the 'canonicalize then compare' idea from Valid Anagram, but instead of comparing two forms we *index* by the form. The map turns an O(n²) all-pairs comparison into O(n) bucket insertions.

approaches.name: Character-Count Key (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The improvement: replace per-word sorting with O(k) counting.
hints: Sorting each word costs O(k log k). Can you build a canonical key in O(k)?
Two words are anagrams iff their 26-letter counts match. Use those counts as the key.
Encode the count vector into something hashable — a tuple in Python, a delimited string in Java.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each word is scanned once to build a 26-length count (O(k)), and the encoded key is O(26)=O(k) to form/hash. Total O(n·k). Space O(n·k) to store the words.
approaches.explanation:
Instead of sorting, count each word's 26 letter frequencies and use that frequency signature as the map key. Anagrams have identical signatures, so they bucket together — and we avoid the log factor sorting incurred.

**Encoding the key.** The count array itself isn't directly hashable as a map key in Java, so encode it as a string like `"1#0#0#...#2"` (counts separated by a delimiter to avoid ambiguity, e.g. 1,12 vs 11,2). In Python a `tuple(count)` is hashable and clean. Either way, equal signatures ⇒ same bucket.
approaches.insight: The count signature *is* the histogram from Valid Anagram, reused as a dictionary key. Trading the sort for a linear count is the canonical micro-optimization interviewers look for once you've shown the sort solution.

diagrams.title: Buckets keyed by count signature
diagrams.caption: Each frame shows the groups map after one word.

edgeCases.behavior: Empty word → all-zero count signature → its own single-element group.
Identical words share a signature → one group ["a","a"].

pitfalls: Encoding counts without a delimiter — [1,12] and [11,2] can collide into the same string.
Using the raw int[] as a Java map key — arrays use identity equality, so every word becomes its own bucket.
Recomputing the key when retrieving — compute once per word and reuse.

commonMistakes: O(n²) pairwise anagram checks instead of bucketing by a shared key.
Using a mutable/array key in Java (identity hashing) so groups never merge.
Storing the canonical key in the result instead of the original words.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: int[] as a HashMap key in Java
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Arrays hash by identity, not contents, so two equal count vectors are treated as different keys and nothing groups. Encode the counts as a String (or use Arrays-based wrappers).
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
Map<int[], List<String>> groups = new HashMap<>();
groups.computeIfAbsent(count, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(word);
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
String key = encode(count); // e.g. join with '#'
groups.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(word);

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Ambiguous count encoding
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Concatenating counts without separators makes [1,12] and [11,2] both become "112", merging unrelated groups. Use a delimiter.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: for (int n : count) key.append(n); // "112" is ambiguous

patternNote: Canonical-key bucketing in a hash map. Reach for it on any 'group items that are equivalent under some normalization' problem. The count-signature key is the same histogram used by Valid Anagram and the sliding-window anagram problems.
